title: Your Board Is Wrong About AI
author: Managing the Future
summary: CEOs are being pressured by boards to deploy AI primarily for cost-cutting and margin improvement, but this reflexive approach is dangerous. The author argues that AI-generated value should be allocated across three constituencies — customers, employees, and shareholders — not funneled exclusively to shareholders. Evidence from Gartner and MIT suggests that layoffs tied to AI show no correlation with ROI, while gains come from empowering people, not replacing them.
points: Boards tend to pressure CEOs to route AI value almost entirely to shareholders via headcount reductions, reflecting a short-term Friedman-doctrine reflex.
Customers, employees, and shareholders form a three-legged stool; chronically under-serving any one causes the enterprise to topple.
Gartner survey of 350 large enterprises found ~80% had cut staff tied to AI, yet cuts showed no correlation with ROI.
MIT study found 95% of enterprise generative-AI pilots delivered no measurable bottom-line impact; returns came from giving people better tools, not cutting them.
CEOs who prioritize near-term margin gains risk customers who disengage, employees who distrust, and shareholders who still don't see promised ROI.
The right allocation of AI-driven value differs by company based on pricing power, talent market, and competitive position — not a one-size-fits-all formula.
The CEO's job is to hold the full picture; sustained shareholder value is a consequence of serving all three constituencies well.
quotes: Many CEOs turn to layoffs to demonstrate quick AI returns; however, this disposition is misplaced. Workforce reductions may create budget room, but they do not create return. —Helen Poitevin, Gartner analyst
For my team, the cost of compute is far beyond the costs of the employees. —Bryan Catanzaro, VP of Applied Deep Learning at Nvidia
